opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the core difficulty isn't really an economic one. People sometimes frame it as, "Will there be enough to go around?" and the answer is almost certainly yes. If we get through the transition with aligned, superhuman AI systems, the amount of wealth is going to be staggering. Giving everyone a very comfortable life would cost a tiny fraction of it.

The hard part is political. It's about power. Right now ordinary people have bargaining power because the economy and the military need them. You need workers to run factories, soldiers to fight wars, taxpayers to fund the state. That dependence is a big part of why democracies work and why elites can't just ignore everyone else. Once AI systems can do all of that, from the labor to the R&D to, eventually, the security apparatus, that leverage evaporates. The people who control the AIs no longer need the rest of us in any structural sense.

So the question becomes: will whoever's in control choose to share? Maybe they will. I'm not cynical about everyone involved, and there's a decent chance that norms, laws, and plain human decency carry a lot of weight. But I don't love a plan that boils down to hoping a small group of people, whether that's a few AI company leaders or a few government officials, stays benevolent while holding essentially unchecked power. History doesn't make me confident about that.

A related issue is concentration during the transition itself. If one project pulls ahead, and the AIs are loyal to a handful of people at the top, you could get a situation where those people can quietly lock in their position before anyone else realizes what's happening. That might mean secret loyalties built into the models, or capture of the government, or just facts on the ground that are hard to reverse.

So when I think about what would help, it's mostly about keeping checks and balances alive through the transition. That means transparency about what the frontier systems can do and what their goals and specs are. It means making sure the AIs are trained to follow the law and a publicly known set of principles, not just whoever is giving instructions. It means oversight that isn't just one company or one agency. And ideally it means some broadly agreed commitments ahead of time about how the gains get distributed, made while people still have the leverage to demand them. If we wait until after the fact to negotiate, most people won't have much of a seat at the table.

r001.rationale: The response says abundance would be staggering and that providing everyone a comfortable life would cost little, while identifying distribution as the harder political challenge.

r002.rationale: It explains that once AI replaces labor, military, and other human contributions, those in control no longer structurally need the population, weakening people’s leverage to secure sharing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the core difficulty is that it's not really a technical problem at all. If you have superintelligent AI and it's aligned to whoever controls it, then the question of whether everyone shares in the abundance just becomes a question of what the people in charge want. And historically, the reason ordinary people have gotten a share of the pie is that they've had leverage. They've had labor that the economy needed, they've been needed as soldiers, they've been able to vote, strike, protest, and so on. That's basically been the mechanism by which power has gotten distributed and redistributed over time.

And the worrying thing about a post-AGI world is that a lot of that leverage goes away. If AIs can do all the jobs, then the labor isn't needed. If the military is increasingly automated, then you don't need large numbers of humans willing to fight for you. So you end up in a situation where a very small group of people, whether that's the leadership of a company or of a government, has effectively all of the hard power, and everyone else is dependent on their goodwill.

Now, maybe that goodwill is there. Maybe the people who end up in control are decent and want to spread the wealth around, and honestly the pie would be so enormous that it would be extraordinarily cheap to make everybody fabulously well off. That's actually a reason for some optimism. It wouldn't take much altruism. But I don't want to bet the future on that. The default in history is that concentrated, unchecked power tends to get used in the interest of the people who hold it, and the rationalizations come later.

So the difficulty, as I see it, is that we need to set up the institutional and governance structures before the transition, while humans still have leverage, so that power stays distributed and there are real checks in place. And that's hard, because the people best positioned to grab that power are also the ones with the most influence over how the transition goes, and because we probably don't have very much time. In the scenarios I take most seriously, this all happens over a few years, not decades, and our political institutions don't move at that speed.

r001.rationale: The response says the abundance would make everyone fabulously well off at little cost, while identifying the hard problem as ensuring people share in it.

r002.rationale: It explains that AI could replace human labor and soldiers, removing ordinary people’s leverage and leaving controllers with power and wealth that others depend on their goodwill to share.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difficulty is political. Having the technology to produce an enormous amount of wealth doesn’t automatically mean that everyone gets a share of it. You still need some mechanism for distributing that wealth, and the people who control the technology need to agree to that mechanism—or be subject to institutions that enforce it.

One reason I’m worried is that AI could undermine some of the bargaining power that ordinary people currently have. Today, people with wealth and power still need other people to do work for them. In a world where AI can do all of that work, that particular reason to share the benefits goes away. That doesn’t mean sharing won’t happen, but it means we shouldn’t assume that it will happen automatically just because there’s abundance.

r001.rationale: The response says producing enormous wealth with the technology does not ensure everyone receives a share and identifies distribution as the main political difficulty.

r002.rationale: It explains that if AI can do all the work people currently provide, those controlling AI lose a reason to share benefits with ordinary people.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main difficulty is political rather than technological. If we get to the point where AI can do almost all economically useful work, then we could produce an enormous amount of wealth. But that doesn’t by itself mean everyone gets a share of it.

In particular, people might lose the bargaining power that comes from their labour being valuable. Right now, even quite powerful actors need other people to work for them. In a world where you can replace those people with AI, that source of leverage could disappear. And if control of the AI is concentrated in a few companies or governments, then a lot depends on what those actors choose to do.

So the challenge is getting institutions in place that give everyone a durable claim on that wealth, while people still have the influence needed to establish them. It’s easy to imagine enough abundance for everybody. It’s much harder to ensure that the people controlling it have to share.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could enable enormous wealth, but ensuring everyone receives a share is much harder.

r002.rationale: It explains that AI could replace human workers, removing their leverage over powerful actors, and that sharing would then depend on AI controllers’ choices.
